rules.title: Passport Strategies — one per auth method, no more
rules.summary: One huge Strategy with `if`s = you can't add a new auth method without risking the existing ones.
rules.rationale: NestJS + Passport invites `JwtStrategy`, `LocalStrategy`, `ApiKeyStrategy`. Each lives in its own file, and makes no business decisions.

rules.title: Authorization = Policies, not decorators sprinkled across the code
rules.summary: Authorization lives in testable policy functions — not scattered `@RequireRole` decorators on controllers.
rules.rationale: Not `@RequireRole('admin')`, not `@CanAccess('sites:write')` on the controller. A permission is a question about a user and a resource, and the answer lives in a policy function you can test and reuse.

rules.title: Authentication and Authorization are two different layers
rules.summary: Authentication (who you are) and authorization (what you may do) stay in separate guards and services.
rules.rationale: Authentication = who you are. Authorization = what you can do. They don't live in the same guard, and they don't live in the same service. Mixing them is the source of the most painful security bugs.

rules.title: `forRootAsync` for modules with dependent configuration
rules.summary: Hard-coded module config — environments differ only by editing code.
rules.rationale: A module that needs configuration (DB connection, API key) provides a static `forRoot` / `forRootAsync`. Without it, you slide back to singletons and global state.

rules.title: Configuration via ConfigModule, not `process.env`
rules.summary: Inject ConfigService — services never read `process.env` directly.
rules.rationale: NestJS provides `@nestjs/config` with schema validation. Use it. Services receive an injected `ConfigService` — they don't read `process.env` directly. (This is the NestJS expression of rule 16.)

rules.title: OpenAPI / Swagger is generated from code, not maintained by hand
rules.summary: Generate OpenAPI from controllers and DTOs — the spec follows the code, not a hand-edited file.
rules.rationale: `@nestjs/swagger` generates an OpenAPI spec from DTOs and decorators. That spec is the source for the frontend client codegen (see `professional-architecture-testing-contracts` rule 15).

rules.title: Background jobs and events — inside the owning domain
rules.summary: Background jobs enqueue from the domain that owns the work — callers must not know another domain's queue shape.
rules.rationale:
If a domain needs async work (send an email, fire a webhook, recompute statistics), it defines the job inside its own module. Another domain does not push a job onto domain X's queue.

Cross-domain communication via events — a typed event bus, not a direct call into another module's job.

rules.title: Errors — NestJS exceptions, not `throw new Error`
rules.summary: Map domain failures to NestJS HTTP exceptions — clients and logs get consistent, classifiable errors.
rules.rationale:
Throwing `BadRequestException`, `NotFoundException`, `ForbiddenException` lets NestJS map to the right HTTP status. `throw new Error()` collapses to a generic 500 and hides real failures.

Even better: domain exceptions mapped by a NestJS exception filter to a unified error format. The service doesn't know about HTTP — it throws domain errors. The filter maps.

rules.title: Repository pattern — don't expose the ORM to services
rules.summary: Tomorrow you swap TypeORM for Prisma or vice versa — change the repository only, services don't move.
rules.rationale: A service does not receive `Repository<Site>` from TypeORM or `PrismaClient`. It receives a `SitesRepository` you wrote — a clear interface.

rules.title: Transactions sit at the use-case boundary, not inside a repository call
rules.summary: Transactions start and end at the use-case service — not in repositories or controllers.
rules.rationale: `@Transactional` or unit-of-work wraps a service-level call, not a single repository call. If an operation needs two repositories — the transaction lives in the service.

rules.title: Guards and Interceptors — cross-cutting infrastructure, not business logic
rules.summary: Guards authenticate and gate access — business rules stay in services where they can be tested.
rules.rationale:
A `Guard` answers "is this request allowed?" — it does not run business operations, doesn't query several tables, doesn't change state.
An `Interceptor` wraps the response (logging, error mapping, transformation) — it does not make business decisions.

rules.title: Cross-module communication via exported services, not repositories or DB
rules.summary: The repository is internal to the domain. The service is the public API.
rules.rationale: If `WorkspaceModule` needs catalog information, it does not inject `CatalogRepository` or hit the DB directly. It injects the `CatalogService` exported by `CatalogModule`.

rules.title: Every domain is a standalone NestJS Module
rules.summary: Domain logic trapped in AppModule — libs stay empty shells.
rules.rationale: In Nx + NestJS, a domain becomes a `Module` that lives in `libs/<domain>/backend-feature-*` (or similar). The backend `app` only assembles those modules in `AppModule`.

rules.title: DTOs in controllers, entities in repositories — never mixed
rules.summary: Controllers accept and return DTOs — never ORM entities that expose your DB schema.
rules.rationale: The controller takes a DTO from the client and returns a DTO. The service works with domain models. The repository maps to the ORM entity. Every conversion is intentional.

rules.title: Agent runs are a resource, not an ephemeral stream
rules.summary: An agent run is a persisted resource with an ID and lifecycle — the SSE stream is a window into it, not the run itself.
rules.rationale:
An agent run (the text streaming to the user) is a resource with an ID — not just a passing stream. It is persisted in the DB with state (`pending`, `running`, `completed`, `failed`, `canceled`), accumulated output, and tool calls. The stream is a window into the resource, not the resource itself.

Implementing this rule requires a **documented disconnect policy** (see the cancellation modes in the related LLM-streaming rule). Explicit cancel (`DELETE` / Stop button / `POST .../cancel`) must exist regardless of the chosen policy. Client resume must not be broken by a naive `req.on('close')` abort.

rules.title: Heartbeats and reconnect — part of the protocol, not an add-on
rules.summary: Heartbeats and reconnect belong in the transport protocol from day one — not as a later patch.
rules.rationale:
- **SSE**: emit an empty comment (`:heartbeat\n\n`) every 15–30 seconds; on reconnect the client sends `Last-Event-Id` to resume.
- **WebSocket**: rely on ping/pong (socket.io does this automatically) and exponential backoff on reconnect.
- For durable runs, pair heartbeats with explicit cancel/resume policy (see related streaming rules).

rules.title: Idempotency keys on every agent action
rules.summary: Require an Idempotency-Key on run creation — retries and double-clicks return the same run.
rules.rationale: The client sends an `Idempotency-Key` header on every run-creation request. If the request arrives twice (network, retry, double-click) — the server returns the same run, doesn't create a new one.

rules.title: LLM streaming — cancellation and backpressure are mandatory
rules.summary: Cancel downstream LLM work when the client disconnects and apply backpressure when it cannot keep up.
rules.rationale:
The user closes the tab mid-response? The upstream LLM call must abort. The server stops paying.
The LLM emits faster than the client can consume? Push backpressure.

**Cancellation mode depends on run durability.** The example below applies to **ephemeral streams** — no durable run, no Redis resume. When the run is durable/resumable (see related rules), HTTP disconnect is not always abandonment, and `req.on('close')` → abort breaks page-refresh resume.

| Mode | When | Cancel on HTTP disconnect? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Ephemeral** | One-shot SSE, no resume | Yes — `req.on('close')` → abort |
| **Durable / resumable** | Run persisted, Redis buffer, `GET .../stream` resume | Ask the user — product trade-off, not a fixed default |
| **Cost guard** | Durable + idle timeout | Abort if no consumer reconnects within N minutes |
| **Explicit only** | Host opts into cost-first | Only `DELETE` / Stop aborts |

Page refresh and tab close look **identical** to the server (TCP drop). Backpressure (propagating consumer slowness to the LLM stream) applies in **both** modes regardless of the chosen cancel policy.

rules.title: Tool calls and agent output — structured events, not free text
rules.summary: Free-text streams can't drive UI state for tool calls, errors, or completion.
rules.rationale: An agent's response streams as a sequence of typed events: `text-delta`, `tool-call-started`, `tool-call-completed`, `tool-call-failed`, `run-completed`. Not free text the client has to parse.

rules.title: Tool outputs defined by schema, not blocklist sanitization
rules.summary: Every agent tool declares an outputSchema; enforce at build time and validate at runtime — never strip internal fields with a growing block list.
rules.rationale:
Every tool declares an explicit `outputSchema` (Zod or JSON Schema). The schema is the allowlist: only declared fields are persisted and returned.

1. **Build-time enforcement** — registering a tool without `outputSchema` fails CI (or module load in dev). No exceptions for "internal" tools.
2. **Runtime validation** — parse tool output against `outputSchema` before persistence and before emitting `tool-call-completed` events.
3. **No blocklist sanitizer** — do not maintain a shared `INTERNAL_KEYS` list on run results, messages, or tool calls. If a field should not reach clients, it must not be in the schema.

Provider-only metadata stays inside the LLM adapter layer and never enters the tool execution boundary.

rules.title: Rooms and channels — always namespaced by domain and tenant
rules.summary: Namespace room names with tenant or org scope so realtime events never cross tenants.
rules.rationale: A room in `socket.io` or a topic in a message broker must include the tenant. `room: doc-123` is wrong. `room: org-456:doc-123` is right.

rules.title: Scaling real-time — via Redis adapter, not in-memory
rules.summary: Use a Redis adapter so WebSocket and SSE events reach clients on any app instance.
rules.rationale:
The moment you have more than one server instance, you can't keep connections in process memory. Redis (or similar) is the broker that fans events between instances. After wiring, `server.to(roomId).emit(...)` reaches every instance and every user in the room.

For **SSE resumable streams**, the same Redis (or similar) broker lets instance B serve a `GET .../stream` resume when instance A handled the original `POST /stream`. That satisfies this rule for cross-instance relay — it does **not** require keeping the LLM alive after disconnect. Relay + abort-on-idle is valid.

rules.title: Pick one mechanism per flow — don't confuse SSE with WebSocket
rules.summary: Use SSE for one-way LLM token streaming — reserve WebSocket for bidirectional chat.
rules.rationale:
- **SSE (Server-Sent Events)** — one-way stream from server to client. Ideal for LLM token streaming, job progress, notifications.
- **WebSocket** — bidirectional. Required only when the client sends frequent unsolicited messages (collaborative editing, user-to-user chat).
- **Long polling** — fallback, not default.

rules.title: WebSocket Gateways — thin transport, not business logic
rules.summary: The gateway is transport, not business logic. It receives a message, authorizes, hands off to a service.
rules.rationale: In NestJS, a WebSocket gateway has one responsibility. It does not share state with controllers, and business logic does not live inside it.

rules.title: WebSocket auth — at handshake, not per message
rules.summary: Authenticate WebSocket connections at handshake — not with JWT verification on every message.
rules.rationale: On `connect`, the client sends a token (in `socket.io` `auth`, in a query, or in `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`). If invalid → immediate disconnect. Each subsequent message reads the user from the socket context.

rules.title: Error boundaries per domain
rules.summary: Wrap each domain's UI in an error boundary — one widget crash must not blank the whole shell.
rules.rationale: A crash in one domain does not take down the app. Each domain wraps itself in an Error Boundary that knows how to display failure sensibly for that domain.

rules.title: Migrations are part of the domain
rules.summary: Each domain owns its database migrations — no cross-domain schema edits.
rules.rationale:
A DB migration lives in the domain's `data-access` lib. One domain doesn't touch another's tables. A schema change = a PR inside that domain, not in infrastructure.

Foreign-key direction matters: the **consumer** holds the link to the **owner**, not the other way around. If workspace needs to link a workflow to a catalog item, the FK lives on `workflows.item_id` — not on the catalog table.

rules.title: Observability is infrastructure, not an add-on
rules.summary: Standardize logs, metrics, and traces per domain so production incidents point to the right team.
rules.rationale: Logs, metrics, and traces come out of one shared platform library. Every domain uses it — does not roll its own. Every log carries `domain` and `requestId` by default.

rules.title: Always authorize on an object loaded from the DB, not on user input
rules.summary: Load the resource from the DB and authorize against it — never trust IDs from the request body alone.
rules.rationale: The user sends `siteId`. You don't authorize on the ID — you load the site and authorize on the loaded object. If it doesn't exist — `NotFoundException`. Only then check whether the user may act on it.

rules.title: Secrets don't sit in code or logs
rules.summary: Secrets live in env or secret stores — never in source, committed config, or client bundles.
rules.rationale: API keys, JWT secrets, DB passwords — only via `ConfigService`. And never in logs. A logging interceptor strips dangerous values automatically.

rules.title: Rate limiting and CSRF are infrastructure, not optional
rules.summary: Rate limiting and CSRF ship as shared infrastructure — wired once, not bolted on per route later.
rules.rationale: `@nestjs/throttler` on every endpoint. CSRF token on every state-changing operation from a cookie-based client. Baseline headers via `helmet` by default. All three ship as global infrastructure — wired once in `AppModule` / `main.ts`, not bolted on per route later.

rules.title: Multi-tenancy — tenant is a required scope, not a reminder
rules.summary: Every query scopes to the current tenant — authorization filters belong in the data layer, not just the controller.
rules.rationale: If you have organizations/accounts, every query is filtered by tenant automatically. Not "remember to add `where: { orgId }`" — that will fail. Use `RequestContext`, `AsyncLocalStorage`, or row-level security in the DB.

rules.title: Backend ↔ frontend communication via a generated client, not `fetch`
rules.summary: Hand-written fetch — API changes fail in the browser, not at compile time.
rules.rationale: Every domain with a backend produces a client (OpenAPI / tRPC / GraphQL codegen) as part of its `data-access` lib. The frontend does not write `fetch('/api/...')` by hand.

rules.title: Every library has one purpose — feature, data-access, ui, or util
rules.summary: Mix UI with API in one lib — Storybook needs the whole stack mocked.
rules.rationale: In Nx this is the `type` tag, not just convention. A library that mixes UI with API calls with business logic is a library you can't understand, test, or delete.

rules.title: No shared global state
rules.summary: No module-level mutable singletons — state injects at app entry so domains can run standalone.
rules.rationale: No singletons holding cross-domain state. No global store every app writes to. If two domains need the same data, one owns it and the other receives it via the public contract.

rules.title: Dependencies flow one direction
rules.summary: Dependencies flow one way: apps → feature → data-access → shared — shared never imports a domain.
rules.rationale:
Layering: `apps → features → data-access/ui → util/shared`. `shared` may not know about a specific domain. `ui` may not import `feature`. Nx enforces with `type:` tags.

`shared` provides a mechanism (a registry, an interface, a base class). The domain registers into it from its own app entry point. `nx graph` shows flow goes one way.

rules.title: Clear server vs client boundary
rules.summary: Tag every lib `scope:server`, `scope:client`, or `scope:isomorphic` — enforce at the bundler boundary.
rules.rationale: In a monorepo with backend and frontend apps, every library must declare which side it runs on. A "both" library is one the bundler will catch importing `fs` in production. Tag libs `scope:server`, `scope:client`, or `scope:isomorphic` and enforce via `enforce-module-boundaries`.

rules.title: Full separation between domains
rules.summary: Every domain is a standalone app with its own backend, frontend, and tests — runnable alone, with no cross-domain shell.
rules.rationale:
Every domain is a standalone app: own backend, own frontend, runnable alone. The test: I want to work on catalog — I bring up that app alone, open the browser, and work. No workspace, no workflow builder, nothing else.

Verification: `nx serve catalog` runs with zero connection to workspace. `nx graph` shows islands, not a pile.

rules.title: Raise the friction for adding a new domain
rules.summary: Every new feature shouldn't become its own domain — a domain is a business capability, not a widget.
rules.rationale: Creating a new domain is not a casual decision. It requires tech review, a defined owner, a README, and a CODEOWNERS entry. A domain is a commitment.

rules.title: Explicit cross-domain contracts via Nx tags
rules.summary: Cross-domain imports go through public barrel exports — Nx tags enforce who may depend on whom.
rules.rationale: A domain may not import from `src/` of another domain. Only via the library barrel (`index.ts`). Nx enforces this with tags.

rules.title: Full test isolation
rules.summary: Domain tests boot only their domain — not the whole platform graph.
rules.rationale:
`nx affected:test` is the default. CI runs only the tests for what changed. Each domain's tests use that domain's code only — no cross-domain `setupX()` helpers or unrelated mocks.

A test that needs the whole system up = red flag the architecture is wrong.

rules.title: Documentation in a place you can't miss
rules.summary: Every domain lib ships a README — ownership, boundaries, and how to run it alone.
rules.rationale: Every app has a README. Every feature lib has a README. It explains: responsibility, public API, how to run alone, external dependencies.

rules.title: Build artifacts are per-domain
rules.summary: Each domain produces its own build artifact — deploy, rollback, and monitor independently.
rules.rationale: `nx build sites-management` produces a standalone artifact. You can deploy it alone, roll it back alone, monitor it alone.

rules.title: CODEOWNERS reflects the boundaries
rules.summary: Without it, someone "just" tweaks the core at 2 AM and three domains break by morning.
rules.rationale: Map `.github/CODEOWNERS` per domain. A PR touching `libs/studio/*` requires Studio-team approval. A PR touching `libs/shared/*` requires platform-leads approval.

rules.title: Configuration is read at the entry point, not in the middle of the code
rules.summary: No surprises. All settings in one reviewable place.
rules.rationale: `process.env.X` or `import.meta.env.X` appears in one place — the app's config file. The rest of the code receives typed values, doesn't read env vars directly.

rules.title: Schemas and types — one source of truth
rules.summary: Shared types live in one library — server and client import the same schema.
rules.rationale: The `Site` type isn't written twice. It lives in one library (usually `data-access` or a dedicated schemas lib), and both server and client import from it.

rules.title: Testing — three tiers, not one
rules.summary: Three test tiers — unit, integration, e2e — so CI stays fast and a red test names the broken layer.
rules.rationale:
NestJS invites writing everything as e2e with `Test.createTestingModule`. That's a mistake. Three tiers:

- **Unit** — service or utility, no NestJS DI, mocks by hand. Fast, focused.
- **Integration** — module wired up with `Test.createTestingModule`, real DB (testcontainers), no HTTP. Verifies wiring.
- **E2E** — full app with `supertest`. Verifies public contracts.

rules.title: Composition, not inheritance
rules.summary: UI libs receive behavior via props and slots — they do not pull from app context.
rules.rationale: UI libs do not inherit behavior from context. They receive it — as props, as children, as render-props, as slots. The parent decides how to assemble; the child only knows how to render.

rules.title: Configuration, not conditionals
rules.summary: Host-specific behavior passes in as props — shared libs do not sniff where they run.
rules.rationale: Same library, different behaviors per host — through props and configuration, not `if`s that sniff where the code is running.

rules.title: Feature flags instead of code branches
rules.summary: Without flags, every deploy waits on a coordinated release.
rules.rationale: A new capability ships behind a flag. The flag is controlled from outside (configuration, not code). When the capability is mature — delete the flag, do not leave it "just in case".

rules.title: Version your public contracts
rules.summary: Version public data-access exports — breaking changes ship as v2, not silent rewrites.
rules.rationale: The `data-access` lib of a domain is a contract. A breaking change to its public API = a new entry, not a delete of the old one. Consumers migrate at their own pace.
